claim: Random 3-SAT has a sharp hardness peak near clause/variable ratio 4.27 for DPLL-style solvers; hard instances are about half satisfiable.
agent_test: Not an agent test; used to design tests: sweep alpha for our agent's SAT task.

claim: Unit propagation and clause learning (CDCL: GRASP, Chaff, MiniSat) turned DPLL into an industrial tool; Chaff reported one to two orders of magnitude speed-up over GRASP and SATO, credited to engineering (watched literals, VSIDS).
agent_test: Compare an agent that applies all forced consequences with code before each guess versus one that reasons them in text, equal tokens.
audit_note: 'Turned DPLL into an industrial tool' is a narrative gloss only weakly supported (Wikipedia says CDCL made solvers powerful for real-world applications, tagged citation needed); Chaff's one-to-two-orders speed-up over GRASP/SATO and its engineering credit are exact.

claim: Keeping learned clauses chosen by a cheap quality score (LBD) beats keeping all or by length; low-LBD clauses are reused far more often.
agent_test: Score memory notes by a cheap reuse proxy and keep the top few; compare with keeping all notes at equal context.

claim: A SAT proof can be a checkable certificate: the Pythagorean triples proof (n=7825) used cube-and-conquer, about 4 CPU years, and a DRAT proof of almost 200 TB (68 GB compressed) that an independent checker verified.
agent_test: Require the agent's UNSAT-style claims to ship with a machine-checkable certificate and have a separate checker run it.

claim: Non-reasoning LLMs (GPT-4, GPT-4o, Gemini 2.0 Flash, Claude 3.7, DeepSeek V3) show an easy-hard-easy accuracy curve on random 3-SAT, dropping to about 10% in the hard region, and few-shot examples do not fix it. Contested: Zhang et al. 2026 find most models (except GPT-5) do not show the easy-hard-easy shape at all and instead say SAT almost always; Hazra 2024 and 2025 are the same group. Verma 2026 adds that density and solver hardness are confounded; matched-density Tseitin pairs with a 10x-50x conflict ratio do not order accuracy (pooled gap +1.7 points, p=0.74).
agent_test: Run our agent on 3-SAT search at alpha 3, 4.27, 6 with n<=10 and compare plain, CoT, and scaffold at equal tokens.

claim: DeepSeek-R1 is the exception on small 3-SAT: hard-region accuracy beats other LLMs easy-region accuracy, accuracy is flat in the satisfying-assignment ratio, and thinking tokens rise in the hard region.
schema_part: S4/O (spend more thinking on hard cases)
agent_test: Check whether our agent allocates more tokens to hard-region items and whether accuracy stays flat across model-count ratio.

claim: Letting the LLM translate the problem to CNF and a SAT solver decide gives about 100% on 3-SAT across all alpha, versus about 10% for direct LLM search in the hard region. Boundary: this holds on clean CNF. On real text the translation step loses accuracy: in legal NLI the real Z3 pipeline scored below plain LLM classification for 4 of 5 models (Claude 74.5 vs 63.1 is the exception), and without a faithfulness reward answer accuracy was 91.2 but formula equivalence only 80.6.
agent_test: Compare direct solving with translate-then-solve on the same items at equal total tokens.

claim: Solver-aided prompting (LLM writes declarative constraints, Z3 solves) beats chain-of-thought and imperative program-aided prompting on constraint tasks with code-davinci-002 (GSM-SYS 69.4 vs CoT 46.5 vs ProgLM 43.4; LSAT 35.0 vs 23.5; BoardgameQA 79.4 vs 60.7). Update 2026: with current models (GPT-5, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Claude Sonnet 4, DeepSeek-Reasoner) the solver gain over zero-shot CoT is under 1% on near-ceiling deduction sets (GPT-5 average -0.13), but solver pipelines keep 76.7% vs 62.2% accuracy at 14-17 reasoning steps. LSAT, BoardgameQA and GSM-SYS were not re-run.
agent_test: Replicate on our own constraint puzzles with a current model; the gain was measured on an old model.

claim: Solver-aided reasoning is not uniformly better: Logic-LM with GPT-4 was worse than CoT on PrOntoQA (83.2 vs 98.8) but better on ProofWriter, FOLIO, LogicalDeduction and AR-LSAT; gains come mostly when formalisation succeeds.
schema_part: O (route to solver only when it fits)
agent_test: Add a router: use a solver when the problem is formalisable, otherwise plain reasoning; compare against always-solver.

claim: A solver gives a free error signal (UNSAT, AMBIGUOUS, execution failure) that supports abstention and repair: SatLM selective accuracy 77% vs 45% on GSM-SYS; Logic-LM self-refinement raised executable rate (GPT-3.5 FOLIO 66.7% to 84.3%) but accuracy plateaued after early rounds.
agent_test: Feed tool failure messages back for at most 2 repair rounds and measure accuracy versus extra tokens.

claim: Accuracy on SAT-derived puzzles falls with clause count; UNSAT is much harder than SAT (SATBench hard: SAT 66.7% vs UNSAT 39.3% average; o4-mini 91.1 vs 65.0). The best model is o4-mini at 89.3% overall. SATQuest (2026) agrees: accuracy falls with solver-measured complexity, o3-mini 0.56 and DeepSeek-R1 0.42 overall, with minimal-unsatisfiable-subset tasks among the hardest.
agent_test: Report SAT and UNSAT accuracy separately for every benchmark; add UNSAT-heavy hard items to our test set.

claim: Models show a satisfiability bias: they say SAT too often, and a right label often comes with an invalid trace (o4-mini SAT label 94.7 vs trace 74.6; Claude 3.7 83.2 vs 47.4; satisfiability bias is 68.7% of o4-mini errors).
schema_part: G (check the reason, not only the label)
agent_test: Grade traces by checking the claimed assignment or core against the formula; compare label accuracy to trace accuracy for our agent.

claim: Plain accuracy overstates LLM SAT skill; a matched-pair metric (ADR) that needs a SAT formula and its one-edit UNSAT twin both right shows GPT-5 at 0.79 for 25 variables and 0.35 at 50 (only about 20% of runs finished at 50). Other models sit near 0.5 accuracy past 25 variables.
agent_test: Use minimal-pair items (flip one literal) so that always-SAT guessing scores zero.

claim: Making failure patterns explicit in the prompt corrected 60.4% of o4-mini and 73.2% of DeepSeek-R1 failures on SATBench re-evaluation, more than light LoRA fine-tuning (Qwen2.5-14B 51.9 to 53.6).
agent_test: Add a short checklist of the named failure modes to the scaffold and test on SATBench hard at equal tokens; the correction number is on re-evaluation of failures, not a fresh run.

claim: Decisions on CNF versus Vertex Cover versus 3D packing agree on 75-80% of instances, so skill is partly representation-independent.
agent_test: Present the same item in two encodings and check agreement.

claim: A message-passing network trained on one sat/unsat bit reaches 85% on SR(40) and decodes assignments for 70% of satisfiable cases, and generalises to larger formulas only by running more iterations (25% on SR(200)).
agent_test: Not directly testable on a language agent; relevant as a baseline for learned search.

claim: G4SATBench finds that NeuroSAT and GGNN struggle to generalise across distributions in most cases and show limited generalisation to larger formulas (better when trained on SR), and that GNNs learn a heuristic akin to greedy local search and fail to learn the CDCL heuristic; the original NeuroSAT paper reported more favourable transfer to larger problems when run for more iterations.
agent_test: Warns against reading small-formula success as general reasoning; test our agent at a size beyond the examples.
audit_note: G4SATBench findings are accurate (b09 and b10 are the same paper), but the general claim ignores that the original NeuroSAT paper reports generalisation to larger problems (25% of satisfiable SR(200)) and new domains by running more iterations, and G4SATBench says SR-trained models generalise better.
claim_before_audit: Neural SAT classifiers generalise poorly: G4SATBench finds weak transfer across distributions and larger sizes, and GNNs behave like local search and not CDCL.

claim: Neural guidance inside a strong CDCL solver gives small gains, and the headline NeuroCore gain was largely a refocusing effect: random logits (rand-glucose) matched neuro-glucose on SATCOMP-2018; on scheduling neuro-glucose solved 20% more than glucose and rand-glucose 2.5% fewer. NeuroBack gives +5.2%/+3.0% over default Kissat with a random-phase control.
agent_test: Include a random-hint control for every scaffold feature that injects guidance, at equal tokens.

claim: Transformers with chain-of-thought can in principle run DPLL-style backtracking: a constructed model decides 3-SAT with O(p^2) parameters and CoT of 8p to 20p steps; trained models reach 99.8% or more SAT/UNSAT in-distribution but do not length-generalise, and full-trace correctness falls to 86.06% on skewed data with p 11-15.
agent_test: Train-free analogue: ask the agent to write explicit decide/propagate/backtrack traces and verify each step by code.

claim: LLM-driven evolution of SAT solver heuristics gives real but partly tuning-confounded gains: AutoSAT beats MiniSat on 9 of 12 datasets; AutoModSAT reports 40% PAR-2 over baseline ModSAT but tuned Kissat wins on some sets; SATLUTION evolved solvers solved 347/345/344 vs 334 for the 2025 gold solver on the authors' hardware. AESAT (IJCAI 2026) trained on 60 instances: best training gain 36.6% PAR2, but held-out totals over SAT Competition 2022-2025 are 1281-1291 solved vs 1269 baseline (about 1-2% more); it reports winning the 2025 competition main track. No equal-budget tuning baseline in the paper.
schema_part: none (outer loop, relevant to our HTSA improvement loop)
agent_test: Use equal-evaluation-budget comparison against a tuned-parameter baseline when evaluating self-improving loops.
audit_note: Totals 1281-1291 vs 1269 verified; the AESAT paper has no parameter-tuning baseline (no tuning/SMAC mention found).

claim: Accuracy of LLMs on search-heavy CSPs collapses with search-space size and solver conflicts (ZebraLogic: o1-full 81.0 overall; Llama-3.1-405B 1.5 on large and 0.0 on X-large); majority vote helps little (GPT-4o 38.0 at N=32) while oracle best-of-N reaches 60.3.
agent_test: Compare scaffold against best-of-N and majority vote at equal tokens on large puzzles; oracle best-of-N is an upper bound, not a usable arm.
audit_note: Table columns garbled in text extraction but row values match (o1-full 81.0; Llama-3.1-405B large 1.5, X-large 0.0 with overall 32.6; GPT-4o majority 38.0 at N=32 from 31.7, oracle 60.3).

claim: A narrative wrapper costs little for the strongest models (o4-mini puzzle 89.4 vs raw CNF 94.3; DeepSeek-V3 84.0 vs 87.3), and changing GPT-4 input from CNF to a story did not help in the hard 3-SAT region.
agent_test: Test one item in story and formula form; expect small difference for strong models.
audit_note: o4-mini puzzle 89.4 here vs 89.3 overall elsewhere in SATBench (rounding).

claim: Direct reasoning on hard UNSAT formulas fails partly by token budget: at a 16k cap a reasoning model hit the cap on all 28 non-abstained random-UNSAT rows (accuracy 0.036) while solving the satisfiable control at 1.00; at 32k the matched-density gap vanished.
agent_test: Add a stop-and-delegate rule before the budget cap; measure accuracy by budget at 8k, 16k, 32k.

claim: Verdict accuracy depends on surface form for some models: a proof-preserving relabelling lowered accuracy by a mean 93 points in all five clusters for one model but not another; satisfiable pigeonhole lookalikes raised false-UNSAT from 2.1% to 18.8% for Llama 3.3.
agent_test: Run paired-twin items (same logic, new surface) as a shortcut detector.

claim: Letting the LLM narrate a solver run is not the same as running it: scope laundering (solver-style answers without execution) occurred in 15.3% to 52.5% of cases across five LLMs on legal NLI, and the real solver was less accurate than the LLM in 4 of 5 models.
agent_test: Require actual tool output in the trace; compare the narrated answer with the executed answer.

claim: Models fabricate solver calls and abandon reasoning on hard SAT-derived items (o3-mini response length falls on MCS and MUS tasks at high complexity); R1 and QwQ reason in raw DIMACS and drift.
agent_test: Check for shortened traces on hard items as an abandonment signal.

claim: LLM-evolved heuristics shrink on held-out data: a 36.6% PAR2 gain on 60 training instances became about 1-2% more instances solved across four held-out competition years; only 46% of training winners kept their edge on the full sets.
agent_test: Always evaluate evolved prompts on a held-out split with a train/validation/test protocol.

claim: Open after this search: no study tests a prompt-only scaffold with code unit propagation and certificate checks against CoT and best-of-N at equal tokens on random 3-SAT; none tests forced assignment substitution, an LBD-like memory score, or DPLL-vs-local-search trace audits on a current reasoning model.
agent_test: These are our own experiments to run.
